title: Gale's Tools
subtitle: Stabilizer, layers, onion skin and more

lessons.title: The Stabilizer
lessons.summary: Smooth lines, even with shaky hands.

steps.title: Smooth lines for shaky hands
steps.text: Gale's stabilizer works like a string. Your brush sits at the end of an invisible string and only moves when your pencil pulls the string tight. Little shakes never pull it, so they disappear. The orange line is a shaky hand. The dark line is what Gale draws.

steps.title: Try the stabilizer
steps.text: Draw the same wavy line with different stabilizer amounts and compare.

tasks: Set the stabilizer to 0 and draw a slow wavy line.
Turn it up to the middle and draw the same line.
Turn it all the way up. The line trails a little behind your pencil, but it's very smooth.

steps.title: Big spiral
steps.text: Trace the spiral. Turn the stabilizer up if your line gets wobbly.
steps.hint: Draw a bit slower than usual and let the stabilizer smooth it out.

quiz.question: When is a low stabilizer better?
choices: Tiny details and quick, sharp marks
quiz.explain: A strong stabilizer trails behind your pencil and rounds off sharp corners, so turn it down for small, quick details.

steps.title: Clear sheets
steps.text: Layers are like clear plastic sheets stacked on top of each other. Draw the background on one, a tree on another and your character on the top one. Then you can change one without messing up the others.

steps.title: Sketch, then clean up
steps.text: A great trick: do a messy sketch on one layer and turn its opacity down so it's faint. Make a new layer on top and draw clean lines over it. When you're done, hide the sketch layer.

steps.title: Make a sketch layer
steps.text: Set up a sketch layer and an ink layer.

tasks: Open the Layers panel and add a new layer.
Name the bottom layer Sketch and do a quick, loose drawing.
Turn the Sketch layer's opacity down to about 30%.
Add a layer on top called Ink and trace clean lines.
Hide the Sketch layer to see your clean drawing.

quiz.question: Why put a sketch on its own layer?
choices: So you can fade it and hide it later
quiz.explain: On its own layer, the sketch can be faded while you ink, then hidden when you're done.

lessons.title: Onion Skin
lessons.summary: See the frames before and after.

steps.title: See through time
steps.text: Onion skin shows faint copies of the frames before and after the one you're drawing, like looking through thin onion paper. Frames before are blue and frames after are orange. In Gale they're frosted, a little blurry and milky, so they guide you without getting in the way.

steps.title: Slide the ball
steps.text: Draw the ball on each frame. Use the frosted ghost of your last frame to keep the gaps the same.
steps.hint: Each ball should be the same distance from the last one.

steps.title: Set up onion skin
steps.text: Find the onion skin settings in your own project.

tasks: Turn on Onion Skin in the timeline.
Show 2 frames before and 1 frame after.
Switch frosted on and off. Which is easier to draw over?

quiz.question: In onion skin, what does a blue ghost show?
quiz.explain: Blue ghosts are frames that come before. Orange ghosts come after.

steps.title: Animations that repeat
steps.text: A loop is an animation whose last frame leads right back into the first, so it can play forever: a beating heart, a spinning wheel, a walk cycle. Make it once and Gale can repeat it as long as you like.

steps.title: Beating heart
steps.text: Draw the heart growing and shrinking. Frame 4 should lead back into frame 1.
steps.hint: Small, bigger, biggest, a bit smaller, and then it's back to small.

steps.title: Save a loop
steps.text: Turn your animation into a loop you can reuse.

tasks: Animate something that repeats, like your beating heart.
Select its frames in the timeline and choose Save as Loop.
Open a new scene and drop the loop in from the Loops shelf.
Set how many times it plays.

quiz.question: What makes a loop play smoothly?
choices: The last frame leads into the first frame
quiz.explain: When the last frame flows into the first, you can't see where the loop starts.

lessons.title: The Stash
lessons.summary: Save drawings and reuse them anywhere.

steps.title: Keep it, reuse it
steps.text: The stash is a shelf for drawings you want to use again: a tree, a cloud, a prop or a character's head. Gale spots the separate things in your drawing by itself, so you can save each one with a tap and drag it into any frame.

steps.title: Draw a tree to stash
steps.text: Trace the tree. Next you'll save it in your own project.
steps.hint: Draw the bumpy top as one loop, then the trunk lines.

steps.title: Use the stash
steps.text: Fill a scene from your stash.

tasks: Draw a tree, a cloud and a rock in one frame.
Open the Stash. Gale finds each separate thing for you.
Save the tree, then drag it into another frame.
Drag it in a few more times to make a forest.

quiz.question: What is the stash for?
choices: Reusing drawings in other frames and scenes
quiz.explain: Draw it once, stash it, and reuse it as often as you like.

lessons.title: Hair Sway
lessons.summary: Let Gale move hair for you.

steps.title: Hair that moves by itself
steps.text: Hair Sway makes hair move on its own. You circle the hair and draw a line where it grows from (the roots). Gale keeps the roots still and swings the tips the most, with a little wind and gusts, so it looks alive.

steps.title: Roots stay, tips swing
steps.text: Look closely: the tips move a little later than the middle. That delay is what makes hair look soft. Stiff hair moves less and faster. Soft hair swings wide and slow.

steps.title: Make hair sway
steps.text: Try Hair Sway on your own character.

tasks: Draw a character with long hair, with the hair on its own layer.
Pick Hair Sway and circle the hair.
Draw a line along the roots, where the hair meets the head.
Play it. Try more wind, then more stiffness, and see how it changes.

quiz.question: Which part of the hair moves the most?
quiz.explain: The roots are stuck to the head, so the tips swing the furthest.

steps.title: Speed you can see
steps.text: When something moves really fast, a camera sees a smear. Motion blur adds faded copies trailing behind fast things, so your animation feels quick and smooth instead of jumpy. Gale finds what moved and adds the trail for you.

steps.title: Only fast things
steps.text: Motion blur only shows on things that move a lot between frames. Slow things stay sharp. Too much blur makes things hard to see, so keep it subtle.

steps.title: Turn on motion blur
steps.text: Try motion blur on something fast.

tasks: Animate a ball zooming across the screen in 4 frames.
Turn on Motion Blur.
Play it with the amount low, then high. Pick what looks best.

quiz.question: Which needs motion blur the most?
quiz.explain: The baseball moves a long way each frame, so a blur trail helps it read as fast.
